title: Looking back: the practices
hookLine: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem and the gurdwara: which one you kept

cards: New Year's resolutions get announced. The habits that actually last tend to sneak in quietly. A walk after dinner.
A song hummed while washing up. A particular way of saying goodnight. Nobody forced them; they just fit.
Camp three opened a whole toolbox of Sikh practices, one after another. Nobody keeps every tool in daily use. One or two get picked up again and again, and those become yours.

teach.b: Open the toolbox. Seva: service with no audience. Minding shoes at the gurdwara door, washing a dish slowly, setting aside a tenth, teaching someone kindly.
And the warning that came with it: when seva feeds the ego, it stops being seva.
Kirtan: first just listening, then humming, then singing Waheguru to a simple tune, then one line, the rahao, the pause line that holds a hymn's center.
Langar: sitting level on the floor in rows, rolling rotis, receiving with cupped hands, and feeding one person at home with no agenda.

Simran: remembering the Name on the breath, Wahe on the in-breath, Guru on the out-breath, in the early hours before dawn, and the mind running off, again and again, and the practice being only to come back.
Nitnem: the daily banis, Japji at dawn, Rehras at dusk, Kirtan Sohila at night, and the reminder that a starter Nitnem is an invitation, not a test.
And the gurdwara: covering your head, taking off your shoes, bowing to the Word, the warm karah prashad in your hands, the hukamnama read from the page where the Granth is opened.
In Sikh teaching these aren't separate hobbies. They're one life: the Guru's word sung, remembered, served and shared.
Sikhs often sum up Guru Nanak's teaching in three pillars: remember the Name, earn honestly, share what you have.
But a path is walked one step at a time, and one practice can become a door to the others.
So which one stuck for you? Not which one should have. Which one did?

how: Sikhs weave seva, kirtan, langar, simran and Nitnem into ordinary days and gather at the gurdwara; many describe Guru Nanak's three pillars, naam japna, kirat karni and vand chhakna, as the frame that holds them.

games.q: you've been doing seva for months, and people have started praising you for it. you notice you like the praise. what does the path say?
o: stop doing seva, since it's spoiled.
notice the ego, and keep serving without an audience.
do more seva, so people notice more.
games.why: when seva feeds the ego, it stops being seva. the answer is to keep serving, quietly, without an audience.

practice: If it was simran, breathe Wahe in, Guru out; if kirtan, hum a line you remember; if Nitnem, say the first line you know.

If it was seva or langar, picture the task you'll do later and do it now in your mind, slowly and well; if nothing stuck yet, just breathe and let one of them choose you. Whatever it is, give it the whole two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. The year's practices: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem and the gurdwara, and the one that became yours.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service, done with no reward in mind.

carryVoice: Your line: the practice that stuck. One door can open the others. That's three hundred twenty-seven.
